questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real goal of security automation, as the course frames it?
options: To replace the SIEM and SOAR platforms with custom scripts
To reduce the total number of alerts a SOC sees, regardless of accuracy
To remove analysts from the alert-handling process entirely
To get repetitive, high-volume, well-defined work out of analysts' hands so they have time for judgment calls that need a human
questions.explain: The lesson frames automation as freeing analysts from repetitive, high-volume toil so they can focus on judgment-under-uncertainty work, not as a wholesale replacement for analysts.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a good automation candidate, per the three traits covered in the lesson?
options: A task governed by a clear deterministic rule, run at high volume, with low blast radius if it's wrong
A task with low volume but high ambiguity
A task that only occurs once and has never been seen before
A task where the cost of a false negative is unknown
questions.explain: The lesson identifies high volume/low variance, a clear deterministic decision rule, and low blast radius if wrong as the three traits of a good automation candidate.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say isolating a host or disabling an account should not be fully automated without a human checkpoint?
options: Because SOAR platforms do not support those actions
Because those actions always take longer than a human performing them manually
Because those actions are irreversible or high blast-radius, and a wrong call (e.g. isolating a domain controller) can cause serious damage
Because Python cannot technically perform those actions
questions.explain: The lesson specifically calls out irreversible, high-blast-radius actions as needing a human in the loop, even if a script prepares the action.

questions.q: What does the lesson mean by the question: "If this automation is wrong, who notices, how fast, and what does it cost?"
options: A licensing question about which SOAR vendor to buy
A test for deciding whether a step needs a human checkpoint instead of running fully automated
A compliance requirement that must be documented before any script is written
A performance benchmark for how fast a script should execute
questions.explain: This question is presented as a practical test: if nobody would notice a wrong automated action until real damage occurred, that step needs a human checkpoint rather than being fire-and-forget.

questions.q: What pattern does this course say most of its scripts will follow?
options: Python scripts are run manually once and never reused
Python is used only for writing unit tests against existing SOAR playbooks
Python fully replaces SOAR playbooks and takes all response actions autonomously
Python does the high-volume pipeline work (parsing, enrichment, correlation) and hands a decision-ready package to a human or a gated workflow
questions.explain: The lesson describes the course's recurring pattern as 'automate the pipeline, gate the action' -- Python handles parsing/enrichment/correlation, while a human or a gated workflow approves any action.
